Hypercasual Teardown

Blob Merge 3D

Every shot leaves a sticky body behind. You aim numbered jelly blobs from a fixed launcher, they cling where they land, equal neighbours fuse into double value — and the number you build is the key to the chamber floor.

  • Voodoo · developed by Studio 501
  • iOS & Android · since April 2021
  • 10M+ Google Play downloads
  • Free · ads + “No Ads” purchase
  • Endless descent: 128 → 64K and beyond

01One decision: where this blob will stick

Blob Merge 3D looks like a Suika-style drop puzzle, but its verb is different. The launcher never moves: the player chooses a direction, and the blob flies along it before gravity takes over. Because blobs grip whatever they touch first, the direction decides both the next merge and the clutter that stays behind.

ReadThe number in the launcher and the numbers already on the board.
AimDrag: a dotted ray from the fixed launcher rotates toward the target.
LaunchRelease: the blob flies along the ray, then falls.
Stick or mergeIt clings to a wall, peg or blob; an equal neighbour fuses into double value.
Re-readNew value, new score, maybe a lock opens — the next shot starts from that board.
The puzzle is not “where do I drop it” but “what will this blob cling to — and will that be next to its twin?”

Nothing on screen previews the next blob, so each decision is local: read the current number, find its equal, choose a line that reaches it without pasting a small blob in the wrong place. The source supplies small values early (2, 4, 8) and larger feeder blobs later (32, 64 and 128 appear in the late chambers), so the board accumulates a ladder of sizes that rarely line up by themselves.

02The first minute teaches by staging, not by text

The recorded session opens with no tutorial overlay. The first board is arranged so that the obvious shot is correct: an 8 in the launcher, a single 8 on the floor directly below, and a padlock that reads 128.

From first shot to first floor

  1. 0:058 + 8 → 16; the score jumps from 0 to 16.
  2. 0:08–0:40Fours and eights are aimed left and right; some cling to the walls, the rest settle on the floor (fig-aim–fig-score-24).
  3. 1:07–1:0932 + 32 → 64, then 64 + 64 → 128: the padlock lifts.
  4. 1:11–1:14“TOP WORLD” ceremony (fig-top-world), then CONTINUE.
  5. 1:16The same blobs land on the next floor, which asks for 256 and offers a gift lock for 64 (fig-carry-over).

The first chamber takes about seventy seconds and introduces everything except gift locks and obstacles: aiming, sticking, merging, the score and the floor lock. The second chamber adds pegs and the first gift lock at once.

Whether a first-time account sees a hand or text prompt is not established: the recorded client was already set up (a modified, ad-free build by the player’s own account) and the session starts directly on the board.

03Sticky jelly is the identity, not a side effect

Blobs are glossy, squashable bodies with tiny legs. Those legs grip walls and pegs: blobs hang above the pile, cling to the chamber sides and stretch strands to the pegs they touched. A June 2021 App Store review describes sticking walls as something an update introduced, so it is a deliberate rule of the current game, not a glitch.

Sticking changes the arithmetic of the board. A blob does not roll to the lowest point, so the player can deliberately park a value high on a wall and later fire its twin at it (fig-aim → fig-merge-left). It also means a careless shot can freeze a small blob in a corridor that a big pair must pass through. Pegs, bars and the cog in later chambers multiply the surfaces a blob can grab.

Size grows with value: by 4K–32K a single blob spans a large share of the chamber’s width, so late merges depend on where big blobs are hanging rather than on a free path to the floor.

04Locks turn a merge chain into a goal

Each chamber floor carries one padlock and, from the second chamber, one or two gift locks with a gold bow. A lock opens when a merge produces its number; it does not need to be touched. When the last lock on a floor opens, the floor gives way.

What the gift pays

The gift lock’s reward is a big blob in the launcher, worth twice the gift’s number. That pattern repeats every time it was visible: gift 64 → 128 at 1:49; gift 128 → 256 at 3:31 and again at 5:32; gift 512 → 1024 at 5:37 (fig-cog-bigblob shows that 1024 waiting under the score). Later the launcher holds a 2048 and a 4K in the matching chambers. The big blob is a powerful but awkward shot: it can complete a high pair, or it can wedge a huge body into the wrong pocket.

The floor opens only after the last lock

In chamber 3 a 512 formed within seconds of landing and its padlock opened at 2:41 — and nothing else happened. The floor waited almost a minute until a 128 was made for the gift lock; only then came the ceremony and the drop. The padlock is the headline number, but every lock is mandatory.

Bars: time from entering a chamber to its floor opening in one recorded run. Gift locks shown where they were still closed when the floor first came into view (C8 and C9 gifts were not readable). Wherever readable from C4 on, the gifts are exactly a quarter and a sixteenth of the padlock.

The padlock doubles every chamber, while the launcher keeps supplying small blobs. Early floors fall in about a minute; the 16K and 32K floors took roughly five and nine minutes. That growth is the game’s pacing curve — and, as section 05 shows, its weakest point.

05The descent: new geometry, same rules, heavier board

No chamber introduces a new rule. Each one changes the surfaces blobs can cling to and the paths big blobs can take, while the whole previous board falls in with you.

There is no losing — and that is the problem players name

The recorded run never shows a danger line, a countdown or a game-over screen, even with the board around three-quarters full in chambers 8 and 9. The player simply keeps launching until merges trickle through. A Google Play review from April 2023 draws the conclusion: at high values there are “no consequences to just piling in the balls”, so spamming shots eventually merges everything and beats careful aim. The video’s own chapter markers for these chambers are about running out of space and fighting the physics.

The design trades failure for patience: the late game asks for minutes of filler shots rather than good decisions. Any adaptation that wants short, replayable sessions has to give clutter a cost without removing the relaxed, no-punishment feel of the early chambers (Build layer, bridge rows B6–B7).

06Two boosters, and an ad layer wrapped around the launcher

Boosters

Swirl (jelly-bean pinwheel button): a three-to-four-second whirlpool rearranges the whole board and can set off merges between blobs that were apart. Rainbow (swirl-ball button): replaces the launcher blob with a rainbow ball that takes the number of the first blob it touches and merges with it (fig-three-locks). Each started with two charges; when a counter reaches zero the badge turns into an ad sparkle.

The commercial wrapper

  • Bigger-blob offer. A bubble beside the launcher offers four times the current blob for a video: 8 → 32, 4 → 16, 2 → 8, 32 → 128, 64 → 256 in the recording.
  • MERGE button. A rewarded-video button at the bottom right appears from chamber 2. A December 2024 review describes it as pulling a stuck equal pair together — and failing when a third blob sits between them. The white rims on equal pairs (fig-gift-before, fig-crowded) are consistent with that target, though their exact trigger is not shown.
  • Ad breaks and “No Ads”. Store reviews complain about frequent ads, and the App Store lists a single “No Ads” purchase at $2.99; one Google Play reviewer reports that some features still sit behind videos after buying it.

The recorded client served no ads; a grey “Not ready yet” toast appeared once when a booster with an empty counter was tapped.

07Feel: an eleven-colour ladder, squash, and numbers that never hide

The value ladder uses eleven colours and then starts again, so a 4K is red like a 2 and an 8K is yellow like a 4. Size and the white numeral separate the cycles; each padlock wears the colour of its number.

248163264128256512102420484K8K16K32K64K

Colours as they appear on blobs and padlocks in the recording; 64K is seen only on its padlock.

The frames show the visual half of the feedback chain: blobs squash on contact and stretch on pegs, a merge throws a burst of droplets in the new blob’s colour (fig-merge-left), the floor lock lifts away when its number is made (fig-gift-after), and “UNLOCK BIG BLOB!” fills the board centre. The score counts up rather than jumping. Numerals stay upright and white with a dark outline even on deformed blobs, so the board stays readable at a glance.

Sound could not be judged from this material: the narrator talks over the game throughout. A 2021 player review mentions a light vibration on taps. The Build layer therefore treats audio as a design brief, not a copy target.

08Product, audience and reception

A Voodoo-published hypercasual merge game from Studio 501, live since April 2021. Its two-line store pitch promises nothing more than the highest possible score and easy slide controls.

2.9★
Google Play, 13.7K reviews (phone: 2.7★, 10.3K) · looked up 2 Oct 2026
10M+
Google Play downloads · “Contains ads · In-app purchases” · rated Everyone
3.6/5
App Store (US), 2.3K ratings · rated 13+ · “No Ads” $2.99
—
No Steam listing; no Metacritic/OpenCritic page or editorial review found

Reception, read cautiously. Players who praise the game mostly praise the physics — how the blobs bounce, squash and merge is described as mesmerising and satisfying to watch. The low Google Play average sits beside reviews about ad frequency, ads after buying “No Ads”, crashes and the lack of consequence for piling up. Store averages mix all of these and do not measure sales or retention; the gap between the App Store and Google Play figures may reflect different review samples rather than different games.

Audience. The pitch addresses anyone who likes merge-number games; Google Play rates it Everyone, the App Store 13+. One parent writes that a child found it through a YouTuber; another reviewer claims the #1 leaderboard spot after daily play. The design demands little dexterity but growing patience: early floors fall in a minute, late ones in five to nine.

09Development history: a 2021 rework made it sticky

Public developer notes are terse (“Bugs fixes”), but App Store version history and dated player reviews outline how the game changed. Player statements are attributed reports, not verified patch notes.

  1. 17 Apr 2021 · v1.0iOS launch (App Store version history).
  2. 1 May 2021 · player reportThe game froze and crashed on creating a 4096 blob; a flying blob could merge with the one still waiting in the launcher.
  3. 5 Jun 2021 · player reportA reviewer who had reached level 186 returns to a changed game: blobs now stick to the walls, several locks appear, and the numbered-level structure is gone. This matches the ruleset recorded in 2024.
  4. 27 Jan 2022 · player reportWalls are sometimes slippery and blobs fail to stick; when two goal rewards arrive back-to-back, the high blob waiting in the launcher vanishes and is replaced.
  5. 31 Oct 2022 · v2.2“New release”; bug-fix versions follow on 20 Feb 2023, 7 Sep 2023 and 9 Jan 2024.
  6. 17 Dec 2024 · player reportThe MERGE video fails to join two 512Qi blobs blocked by a third — the ladder reaches quintillions.
  7. 18 Dec 2024The analysed run is published (YouTube, itsEntak).
  8. 11 Jul 2025 · v2.4.1 / 2 Dec 2025“Fixes and Improvements” on iOS; Google Play last updated 2 December 2025.

The production lesson is in the 2021 rework: sticking walls and multiple locks turned a plain merge pile into a game about placement and goals, at the cost of upsetting players who liked the simpler version. The recurring bug reports — crashes at new tiers, lost reward blobs, unreliable sticking — become regression tests for any rebuild (AC11–AC13).

10Transferable lessons

  1. Make the aim decide where things stay. A fixed launcher plus sticky contact turns one drag into a placement decision with lasting consequences.
  2. Hide a goal inside the merge chain. Floor locks make “produce this exact number” the objective; gift locks add side goals that pay into the next shot.
  3. Reward with the verb itself. The gift reward is not currency but a bigger blob — more of the core action, with a placement risk attached.
  4. Carry the board forward. Dropping the whole pile into the next chamber makes progress physical and keeps past mistakes in play.
  5. Price clutter. Without a failure state, late chambers reward spam over aim; a short-session version needs a cost for overfilling.
  6. Keep numbers sacred. Upright outlined numerals and an eleven-colour cycle keep a crowded, wobbling board readable.

Build layer — complete mobile web game

This layer is the authoritative specification for building the game. Source behaviour, inferred rules and designed parts are labelled: Verified inspected in frames or sequences of the source recording; Inferred consistent pattern or bounded interpretation; External store pages or dated player reviews; Unknown not established; Designed decision for the adaptation. Reading procedure

  1. Parse this HTML structurally; do not load base64 image data into your text context.
  2. Extract every embedded image to your working directory, naming each file by the id of its enclosing figure; open them with an image tool.
  3. Check that all 21 required figure IDs in the evidence index exist and decode.
  4. Read all of #build-rules, including collapsed sections.
  5. Before coding, compare R2–R4 with fig-aim → fig-score-24, fig-peg-hook, fig-hanging-128; and R8–R10 with fig-gift-before/after, fig-three-locks and fig-carry-over.

Build prompt

Build the complete mobile-first web game specified in this teardown and deliver it as ONE portable HTML file (working title “Sticky Blob Descent”; do not use the original name, logo, art or audio).

Fantasy: you launch squishy numbered jelly blobs with tiny sticky legs into wooden toy chambers. Equal blobs that touch fuse into one blob of double value; you grow them from 2 to thousands and beyond while the chambers carry you ever deeper.

Defining decision: the launch DIRECTION from a fixed launcher at the top. A blob sticks where it first lands — wall, peg, moving bar or another blob — so every shot decides which equal neighbour it reaches now and which space it blocks later (rules R1–R5, episode E1, figures fig-aim → fig-score-24).

Progression: each chamber floor carries a padlock (128, 256, 512 … doubling forever, K/M/B/T… suffixes) and, from chamber 2, gift locks. A merge that produces a lock’s number opens it; a gift pays a “big blob” worth twice its number into the launcher; when the last lock opens, the whole board drops into the next chamber with new geometry (R8–R11, chamber table, fig-gift-before/after, fig-carry-over). Build the ten observed chamber layouts in order, then continue the descent with your own chambers built from the same rules.

Session form: portrait browser window, one thumb — drag to aim, release to launch, drag back to cancel. Swirl and Rainbow boosters are scarce and refilled by play. A chamber is a short goal; overfilling costs a rescue Swirl and then a chamber retry (bridge B6–B7). Progress saves after every settled shot and survives reloads.

Look and feel: brighter, cleaner glossy-jelly toys on warm wood; every number legible on a phone; every merge, lock and big-blob reward understandable with sound off; audio built from the event sheet.

Design the first 20 minutes from the first-session plan. Follow #build-rules for verified rules, design space, mobile bridge, asset direction and acceptance cases AC1–AC21; record your design decisions and actual test coverage. No ads, purchases, invented leaderboards or online features. Plan, build, play-test on a phone-sized viewport and fix within this task — a demo or a single chamber is not completion.

Core statements (must hold in the adaptation)

  • CS1. The player chooses a launch direction for the known launcher blob; it sticks where it first lands, and that position decides which equal neighbour it can touch now and later. Verified
  • CS2. Equal blobs that touch fuse into double value (chains resolve on their own); producing a floor lock’s number opens it; gift locks pay a 2× big blob into the launcher; opening the last lock drops the entire board into a harder chamber whose padlock is doubled. Verified
  • CS3. Clutter accumulates (sticky bodies, ever-larger blobs), so space and adjacency become the constraint; scarce boosters (Swirl, Rainbow) are the only direct fixes. In the adaptation, overfilling has a cost (B6). Verified / Designed cost

Characteristic episode E1 (source 1:41–1:52, chamber 2; fig-gift-before → fig-gift-after): launcher 2; board 16, 32, 64, 32, 2, 128; padlock 256, gift 64. A shot makes 32 + 32 → 64, which immediately merges with the existing 64 → 128; the gift 64 lifts away, “UNLOCK BIG BLOB!” appears and the launcher holds a 128; the padlock 256 remains closed. Score 1196 → 1552 (counting up).

Suggested internal build order (a work plan, not a delivery boundary): physics and sticking → aim/launch → merge and score → locks and floor drop → ten chambers → boosters → overflow/retry → save → presentation and audio → designed chambers → tuning on a phone.

Principles (interpretations from this run)

  • Situations come from residue. Every shot leaves a body that sticks; the chamber’s surfaces decide where residue gathers.
  • Teaching by staging. The first board (8 over 8) and the first gift lock teach the verbs without text.
  • Escalation by doubling. One more doubling per chamber against a slowly growing launcher supply; geometry changes, rules never do.
  • Reward with the verb. Gifts pay bigger blobs, not currency; the ceremony marks depth, and the whole board follows you down.

Art direction and signals

Keep the source fantasy — glossy jelly toys with tiny legs in a warm wooden toy box — and make it cleaner: softer lighting, crisper outlines, slightly larger numerals, stronger separation between the two cycles of the colour ladder (for example a subtle ring pattern on 4K+). Portrait frame: score and depth at the top, launcher just below with free space around it, board in the middle, lock row and boosters at the bottom; nothing may cover the launcher, the aim ray or the lock numbers at the moment of a shot. Anticipation (ray, launcher squash), impact (squash, droplets), recovery (wobble) for every shot; bigger ceremony for gifts and floor drops.

S2 Pre-commit target rimNot in sourceWhile aiming, rim the first blob the ray reaches: green if equal, neutral otherwise. Donor: Hypercasual Teardown — Spinner Merge, rule R06 (target cell outlined green during the drag; Verified, fig-merge-first). Not copied: grid, spinners.
S3 Equal-pair rimWhite rim on separated equal pairs (fig-gift-before, fig-crowded)Kept as a free hint
